primitives.name: NFL Passer Rating (fixed-standard system adopted 1973): four clipped component scores, sum/6 x 100, ceiling 158.3
primitives.verbatim_quote: It is important to remember that the system is used to rate passers, not quarterbacks. Statistics do not reflect leadership, play-calling, and other intangible factors that go into making a successful professional quarterback.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Comp% = 100*C/A [dimensionless, percent of attempts]; C = completions [count]; A = pass attempts [count]; Yds/Att = Y/A [length, NFL yards]; Y = passing yards [length, NFL yards]; TD% = 100*TD/A [dimensionless]; TD = touchdown passes [count]; Int% = 100*I/A [dimensionless]; I = interceptions [count]. Constants carry inverse input units so every term is dimensionless rating points: 30 [percent], 0.05 [rating points per percent], 3 [yards], 0.25 [rating points per yard], 0.2 [rating points per percent], 0.25 [rating points per percent], 2.375 [rating points, dimensionless cap]. clip(x,0,2.375) formalizes the source's printed clamp notes ('award zero points' below floor, 'award 2.375' above cap). a,b,c,d [dimensionless rating points]; Rating [dimensionless, 0 to 158.3 scale]. Dimensional homogeneity: all four components are dimensionless rating points; division by 6 and multiplication by 100 are pure scalars.
primitives.assumptions: Fixed performance standard based on statistical achievements of all qualified pro passers since 1960 (p.314); system adopted 1973, replacing a relative-group ranking method; four categories only: completion percentage, average yards gained per attempt, touchdown percentage, interception percentage; each component floored at 0 and capped at 2.375; average standard 1.000, bottom .000; sum divided by six and multiplied by 100; 158.3 is the maximum; formula applies to any player with at least one pass attempt; worked calibration example printed in source: Aaron Rodgers 2011, 343/502, 4643 yds, 45 TD, 6 INT -> components 1.916, 1.562, 1.793, 2.076, sum 7.348, rating 122.5.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Source-stated exclusion: leadership, play-calling and other intangibles are outside the statistic (rates passers, not quarterbacks). Sensor saturation: completion% >= 77.5, TD% >= 11.875, yards/attempt >= 12.5, or zero interceptions all hit the 2.375 cap, so marginal improvement is invisible; interception% >= 9.5 floors component d at 0. Era non-stationarity: the 1960 fixed baseline predates the 1978 one-contact/head-slap passing liberalization (chronology p.372) and later rule packages, so cross-era ratings are not like-for-like. Small-sample regime: legal at one attempt but statistically meaningless; no attempt-count qualifier inside the formula itself.
timescales: tau_3: season and rule era (1 yr to decades)

layer2.mapping: Bounded observation kernel h: (C,A,Y,TD,I) -> Rating mapping the QB's throw-outcome distribution onto a scalar state estimate in the 22-player dynamical system. The clip() nonlinearity is sensor saturation: above the cap the kernel's Jacobian is zero, so downstream estimators must treat the feature as censored, not linear. Leadership/play-calling are latent state variables the kernel provably does not observe; any Coach-Mind QB model must carry them as separate latent channels rather than imputing them from Rating.
layer2.telemetry: Per-game and per-season C, A, Y, TD, I from play-by-play (all five are directly observable). Calibration anchor printed in source: Rodgers 2011 -> 122.5. Saturation frequency measurable as fraction of qualified seasons hitting any 2.375 cap (source lists top-25 single-season ratings, p.314). Latent leadership/play-calling channels: LATENT_UNIDENTIFIABLE from box-score telemetry alone.

primitives.name: Instant Replay challenge economy: two challenges, conditional third, hard cap at three; timeout-coupled cost; clear-and-obvious reversal threshold
primitives.verbatim_quote: If a team is successful on one of its challenges, it is allowed a third challenge, but a fourth challenge will not be permitted.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: N_max [count of challenges available in a game, dimensionless integer in {2,3}]; k [challenge index, dimensionless count]; indicator function [dimensionless, 0 or 1]; 2 and 3 [challenge counts, dimensionless]. All terms dimensionless counts; no physical units enter. Cost side (stated in prose, not in the equation): one team timeout [count] charged per unsuccessful or illegally initiated challenge; loss of 15 [length, NFL yards] for initiating a challenge after timeouts are exhausted; 10 [time, seconds] runoff after the two-minute warning when a changed ruling would start the clock before the snap.
primitives.assumptions: Challenge must be initiated by the head coach throwing a red flag before the next legal snap or kick; each challenge requires an available team timeout; a team out of timeouts or challenges may not initiate; unsuccessful challenge charges a timeout; illegal challenge charges a timeout; challenge with exhausted timeouts costs 15 yards; only the Replay Official or Senior Vice President of Officiating (or designee) may review plays after the two-minute warning of each half, in any overtime, on any score, on any Try, and on opponent interceptions/fumble recoveries/kicking-team possessions/fourth-down stops/disqualifications; Replay Official reviews are unlimited but must occur before the next legal snap or kick; an on-field ruling changes only on clear and obvious video evidence; all reviewable aspects of a play are subject to reversal even if not the challenged aspect; on reversal the game clock resets to when the ball should have been declared dead; no reset if ruling stands; reviewable play classes enumerated A-J (possession, touching, goal line, boundary, line of scrimmage, line to gain, player count, game administration, disqualification, pass direction/illegal forward pass/field goal/Try/illegal handoff/foreign object).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The clear-and-obvious standard is a high evidence threshold, not a truth oracle: borderline wrong rulings survive review by design. Budget exhaustion creates forced acceptance of possibly incorrect on-field rulings for the rest of the game. The 10-second runoff can terminate a half or game when fewer than 10 seconds remain ('If less than 10 seconds remain in the half or the game, the half or the game is over'); a team timeout avoids the runoff. Judgment fouls outside the enumerated A-J classes are unreviewable. In overtime, coach challenges do not exist at all (p.313): the entire information-purchase channel closes.
timescales: tau_0: play and flag window (before next snap, ~4-40 s)

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to bounded-cost sequential information acquisition (value-of-information / optimal stopping): the coach spends a shared resource (timeouts, which are also clock-management capital) to buy a posterior update from a centralized evidence gate with a high reversal threshold. State vector: (challenges_used, success_flag, timeouts_remaining, clock, score, down/distance). The conditional third challenge is a path-dependent budget expansion: success on either of the first two purchases unlocks one more purchase. The booth's unlimited review channel after the two-minute warning and in OT is a regime switch from decentralized paid sensing to centralized free sensing.
layer2.telemetry: Historical base rates printed p.43: 1986-91 limited system 2,967 plays reviewed / 376 reversals (12.7%); 1999-2024: 8,565 total replay stoppages, 4,876 coaches challenges, 3,604 total reversals (42.1% of stoppages). Per-game observables: challenge flag timestamps, outcomes, timeout states, clock/score context, runoff events. Challenge-level success rate requires joining challenges to reversal logs (the p.43 table aggregates stoppages, not challenge outcomes).

primitives.name: Modified sudden-death overtime (2025 alignment): both teams guaranteed an opportunity to possess even after a first-possession touchdown; 10-minute regular-season cap; defensive score/safety exception
primitives.verbatim_quote: In 2025, NFL clubs approved a rule that aligns the postseason and regular season overtime rules by granting both teams an opportunity to possess the ball even if the first team scores a touchdown, subject to a 10-minute overtime period in the regular season.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: t, tau [time, seconds]; T_max [time, seconds] = 600 s (one 10-minute period) in regular season; T_max = infinity in postseason (15-minute periods until a winner); S_A(t), S_B(t) [points, dimensionless integer counts]; P_A(t), P_B(t) [Boolean: team has possessed or had the opportunity to possess, as defined by the source's kicking-play definition]; D(t) [Boolean: terminal defensive event on the initial possession - defensive touchdown, or safety by the kicking team on the receiving team's initial possession]. Homogeneity: the clock comparison t = T_max compares seconds to seconds; score comparisons compare dimensionless point counts; Boolean terms are dimensionless. Winner at tau: leader in points if both opportunities completed; scoring defense if D occurs on initial possession; tie if t = T_max with equal scores (regular season only).
primitives.assumptions: Coin toss at midfield immediately at end of regulation, visiting captain calls; three-minute intermission; regular season: maximum one 10-minute period, two timeouts per team; postseason: 15-minute periods until winner, essentially new four-quarter contests, three timeouts per half (two OT quarters), two-minute warning in every second and fourth OT period, if tied after two periods a possession ends and the coin-toss loser may choose to kick or receive to start the third period, no extended halftime (short television break then kickoff); 'opportunity to possess' occurs only during kicking plays: a kickoff is an opportunity for the receiving team, a legal kicking-team recovery counts as the receiving team's opportunity consumed, a punt or field goal crossing the line of scrimmage and muffed by the receiving team counts as an opportunity; normal kicking-team touching rules apply; exception: kicking team wins immediately with a safety on the receiving team's initial possession; first possession can also end with a winner if the defense scores a touchdown; if the first team does not score, or the score is tied after both opportunities, the next score by any method wins; disqualified players may not return; instant replay in OT: no challenges, reviews initiated by the replay official only.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Regular-season 10-minute cap creates a tie absorbing state (29 OT games ended tied through 2024, p.312). The guarantee is an opportunity, not a full possession: if the first team's drive plus the second team's opportunity exceeds the remaining clock, the guarantee is truncated by time expiry. Postseason is unbounded: fatigue accumulates without limit (longest postseason OT 22:40, Miami 27 Kansas City 24, 12/25/1971, p.312). A turnover on a non-kicking play does not by itself satisfy the source's kicking-play definition of opportunity. Pre-2025 regular-season and pre-2022 postseason data were generated under different terminal rules and must not be pooled with the 2025 kernel.
timescales: tau_2: OT period (600 s regular season; 900 s postseason)
tau_3: rule era (1958 sudden death; 1974 RS extension; 2010/2022/2025 modifications)

layer2.mapping: Terminal stopping-time kernel over the 22-player possession process: it defines the absorbing states (win_A, win_B, tie) and the path constraint (both opportunities) that every OT simulation roll-out must respect. The 2025 guarantee reweights opening-drive policy: because a first-possession touchdown no longer terminates the game, fourth-down aggressiveness and field-position pinning on the opening drive must be re-derived; the coin toss value collapses toward the safety/defensive-TD exception and the choice of kick direction. In Coach-Mind this is a hard terminal-reward constraint, not a soft feature.
layer2.telemetry: OT scoring summary p.312 (all games through 2024): 457 wins by FG kick, 96 by TD pass, 57 by TD run, 21 by interception-return TD, 5 by fumble-recovery TD, 4 by punt-return TD, 3 by safety, 2 by fake FG/TD pass, 2 by kickoff-return TD, 1 each by fake FG/TD run, blocked-FG returns (kicking team and kicker-recovery variants), blocked-punt return TD; 29 ties. Longest postseason OT 22:40 (p.312); first Super Bowl OT: Super Bowl LI, Patriots 34 Falcons 28, Feb. 5, 2017 (chronology p.382). Per-game observables: coin-toss result, drive charts, clock at each possession change, terminal method.

primitives.name: Postseason/draft tie-breaking: ordered lexicographic cascade with recursive restart semantics and coin-toss terminal arbiter
primitives.verbatim_quote: If, at the end of the regular season, two or more clubs in the same division finish with the best won-lost-tied percentage, the following steps will be taken until a champion is determined:
primitives.latex: T^{*}=\mathrm{first\ }T\in\mathcal{T}\mathrm{\ distinguished\ by\ }f_k,\quad k=\min\{j:\ f_j\ \mathrm{separates\ the\ remaining\ tied\ clubs}\},\quad \mathrm{then\ restart\ at\ }k=1\mathrm{\ on\ }\mathcal{T}\setminus\{T^{*}\}\mathrm{\ in\ the\ applicable\ format}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: T, T* [club identifiers, dimensionless labels]; script-T [set of still-tied clubs]; f_j [j-th criterion value]: j=1 head-to-head won-lost-tied percentage [dimensionless, 0-1], j=2 division percentage [dimensionless], j=3 common-games percentage [dimensionless], j=4 conference percentage [dimensionless], j=5 strength of victory [dimensionless aggregate opponent win percentage], j=6 strength of schedule [dimensionless], j=7-8 combined ranking [integer rank positions, dimensionless; sum of points-scored rank and points-allowed rank, lowest wins, tied clubs share the rank], j=9-10 net points [dimensionless point-count difference], j=11 net touchdowns [dimensionless count difference], j=12 coin toss [Bernoulli(1/2) random bit, dimensionless]. k, j [step indices, dimensionless integers]. All criterion values are dimensionless percentages, ranks, counts, or a random bit; no physical units; comparisons are order comparisons within like-typed criteria only.
primitives.assumptions: Tie games count as one-half win and one-half loss for both clubs (p.36 note). Two-club division order: head-to-head; division %; common games %; conference %; strength of victory; strength of schedule; combined conference ranking in points scored and points allowed; combined all-team ranking; net points in common games; net points in all games; net touchdowns in all games; coin toss. Three-or-more clubs: if two remain after eliminations, restart at Step 1 of two-club format; if three remain after a fourth is eliminated, restart at Step 1 of three-club format. Wild Card: same-division ties use division tiebreaker first; cross-division two-club order starts head-to-head if applicable, then conference %, common games (minimum of four), SOV, SOS, combined rankings, net conference points, net all points, net TDs, coin toss; three-or-more: eliminate all but highest-ranked club per division first (original division seeding preserved for subsequent applications), then head-to-head sweep only if one club defeated each other or lost to each other; wild-card three-club restart goes to Step 2. Only one club advances per tie-breaking step; remaining clubs revert to Step 1 of the applicable format. Combined ranking: add positions in the two categories, lowest score wins; tied clubs each receive the rank as if held solely. Draft: non-playoff clubs select 1-18 in reverse standings; playoff clubs by round of elimination (Wild Card losers 19-24, Divisional losers 25-28, Conference losers 29-30, Super Bowl loser 31, winner 32); ties broken by lowest aggregate opponent won-lost-tied percentage (weakest schedule gets priority), then applicable tiebreakers; two-club ties alternate positions round to round; three-or-more rotate the top club to the bottom of the segment each round.
primitives.breakdown_regime: A single static lexicographic argmax is NOT equivalent to the printed procedure: the recursive restart semantics (and the wild-card three-club restart at Step 2 rather than Step 1) can change which club is eliminated first, so naive implementations mis-seed. Step 12 is an irreducible Bernoulli(1/2) coin toss - deterministic ranking breaks down completely there (historical instance: Carolina won the 1995 draft coin toss with Jacksonville, chronology p.376). Common-games comparisons use percentages because clubs may have played unequal numbers of games (minimum four for wild card). Rank-based criteria (steps 7-8) are discontinuous: an infinitesimal points change can swap integer ranks and flip the outcome. Head-to-head is non-transitive in three-club cycles, which is exactly why the sweep condition and restart rules exist.
timescales: tau_0: single game result feeding the criteria (~3 h)
tau_3: postseason seeding and draft order (annual)

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to a non-Archimedean (lexicographic) multi-objective selector with recursive renormalization: no amount of a lower-priority criterion can outweigh a higher-priority one (point differential cannot veto a head-to-head loss), and the feasible set is re-normalized after every elimination. In the GSE engine this binds as a hard seeding constraint module: standings -> ordered criteria vector -> recursive cascade -> seeds/draft slots, with the coin toss as an explicit random-bit terminal node. Any strength metric that trades criteria against each other (weighted sums, Elo-style scalars) is structurally incompatible with this selector and must be kept out of the seeding path.
layer2.telemetry: All 11 deterministic criteria are computable from final standings, head-to-head matrix, division/conference records, common-opponent sets, opponents' aggregate records, and points for/against (all published in this book's standings and records sections, pp.240-341). Verification: replay the cascade against published historical seeds; coin-toss events are logged league transactions (e.g., 1995 Panthers-Jaguars, p.376).

primitives.name: Emergency Third Quarterback: designation and in-game activation predicate under roster constraints
primitives.verbatim_quote: A Third Quarterback can be activated during a game if the club’s first two quarterbacks are disqualified, injured or undergoing a medical examination.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: u_1, u_2, d [Boolean indicator values, dimensionless 0/1]; QB_i [player identifiers, dimensionless labels]; n_QB^active [count of quarterbacks on the 47/48-player Active List, dimensionless integer]; 3 [quarterback count threshold, dimensionless]; Activate [Boolean transition permission, dimensionless]. All terms dimensionless counts or Booleans; no physical units. Roster context constants (prose): Active List 47 players, or 48 if eight offensive linemen are carried; Inactive List 5 or 6 to complete the 53-player roster; two practice-squad elevations per week may raise the roster to 54 or 55; overall 90-player limit.
primitives.assumptions: Designation is permitted only for a club that does not carry three quarterbacks on its 47/48-player Active List; the designee comes from the Inactive List; activation requires BOTH of the club's first two quarterbacks to be simultaneously disqualified, injured, or undergoing a medical examination; the rule sits inside the Active/Inactive List framework (53-player game roster) with up to two weekly practice-squad elevations; historical active-player limits table (p.44) runs from 16 (1925) through 47/48 (2020-24, 48 if activating eight offensive linemen).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Single-QB unavailability does NOT trigger the rule - the conjunction u_1 AND u_2 is strict. 'Undergoing a medical examination' is a transient state (e.g., concussion evaluation), so activation can be temporary and the roster state oscillates. A club carrying three active quarterbacks has no emergency designation at all - the redundancy channel does not exist for it. The rule covers only the quarterback position; cascading unavailability at other positions has no analogous emergency channel in this text. The cold-start problem (a practice-speed QB entering live game speed) is outside the rule's scope and is not addressed by the source.
timescales: tau_1: in-game activation window (remainder of game)
tau_3: season roster policy and CBA era

layer2.mapping: Redundancy/availability constraint on the QB node of the 22-player dynamical system: it couples the medical/disqualification point process to the roster transition kernel. In simulation, QB availability is a three-state process (QB1 active, QB2 active, emergency QB3 activatable only under the conjunction), and the designation decision at roster-build time is a capacity choice: carrying a third active QB consumes an active slot that could hold another position, while the emergency designation buys a conditional, cold-start option. This is a real-options structure embedded in a hard roster constraint.
layer2.telemetry: Game-day active/inactive lists (published per team in this book's roster sections, pp.46-235), weekly injury/practice reports (reporting cadence defined p.19), QB snap counts per game, disqualification logs, medical-examination durations. Historical activation events are observable from play-by-play QB substitution sequences; the designation itself appears on the game-day inactive list.

primitives.name: 1932 indoor-championship scar -> 1933 codification: hashmarks and forward pass legalized from anywhere behind the line of scrimmage
primitives.verbatim_quote: inbounds lines or hashmarks where the ball would be put in play were drawn 10 yards from the walls that butted against the sidelines
primitives.assumptions: 1932: Bears and Spartans finished in the first-ever tie for first place; an additional game was arranged; moved indoors to Chicago Stadium because of bitter cold and heavy snow; the arena allowed only an 80-yard field reaching to the walls; goal posts moved from end lines to goal lines; hashmarks drawn 10 yards from the walls; Bears won 9-0 on Dec. 18, 1932 on a two-yard Nagurski-to-Grange pass; the Spartans claimed the pass was thrown from less than five yards behind the line of scrimmage, violating the existing passing rule, but the play stood. 1933 (Feb. 25): the NFL, which had long followed college rules, diverged for the first time: hashmarks and goal-line posts adopted, and the forward pass legalized from anywhere behind the line of scrimmage; two divisions with an annual championship game approved July 8.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Pre-1933 invariant set is different: passes restricted by the five-yards-behind-the-line rule, no hashmarks, goal posts on the end lines (before the 1932 improvisation). Any model of pre-1933 play must use the restricted pass-legality region and unrestricted lateral ball placement; pooling erases the discontinuity. The 1932 geometry was venue-contingent (an 80-yard indoor field), not a league invariant - it became invariant only by the 1933 codification. The disputed Nagurski pass shows the pre-codification rule was ambiguous at the boundary (the protest was overruled, not adjudicated by measurement).
timescales: tau_0: single disputed play (1932 championship, seconds)
tau_2: era of play under the new geometry (1933-present)
tau_3: subsequent hashmark relocations (chronology p.366, p.371)

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to a state-space constraint rewrite in the 22-player dynamical system: hashmarks compress the lateral ball-start distribution (the field-position transition kernel gains a concentrated interior source measure instead of boundary-uniform placement), and unlimited pass legality behind the line of scrimmage expands the offensive action set at every pre-snap state. The retrocausal template - venue constraint -> improvised rule -> disputed boundary play -> permanent codification - is the general mechanism by which hidden historical scars become today's 'natural' invariants; any era-aware engine must carry the codification date as a regime-change marker.
layer2.telemetry: Play-location distributions (ball-start lateral coordinates), pass attempts by field zone and down/distance, scoring levels by era (1932 championship 9-0; official statistics kept for the first time in 1932 per the same entry). Hashmark relocation dates are logged in the chronology (pp.366, 371), giving exact regime-change timestamps for historical calibration.

reasoning_traces.think: Start from the resource structure on page 42. A head coach enters a game with two challenge tokens and a finite per-half timeout budget, and the two resources are coupled: every challenge requires an available timeout, and every failed challenge burns one. The conditional third token means the budget is path-dependent: success on either of the first two challenges expands the feasible set from two purchases to three, while failure contracts it. This is not a simple counting problem; it is a sequential decision problem where the state is (challenges_used, success_flag, timeouts_remaining, clock, score, down_and_distance) and the action is whether to spend a shared resource to buy a posterior update from a centralized evidence gate. The gate itself is the second invariant: a ruling changes only on clear and obvious video evidence. That phrase is a threshold on the posterior, not a promise of truth. The coach must therefore model two beliefs at once: his own belief that the on-field ruling is wrong, and his belief about whether the video will clear the booth's high evidentiary bar. These diverge constantly. A coach can be personally certain a spot is wrong by half a yard and still rationally decline to challenge, because the camera angles may not resolve half a yard to the clear-and-obvious standard. The historical base rates on page 43 calibrate the prior: the 1986-91 limited system reversed 376 of 2,967 reviewed plays, about 12.7 percent, while the 1999-2024 coach-challenge era produced 3,604 reversals across 8,565 stoppages, about 42.1 percent of stoppages, though that aggregate mixes booth-initiated reviews with coach challenges. The regime change matters: the early system was booth-driven and conservative; the modern system lets coaches select which plays to contest, which raises the reversal rate through selection effects, not through better cameras alone. Now add the clock physics. After the two-minute warning, a changed ruling that would start the clock before the snap triggers a 10-second runoff, and if fewer than 10 seconds remain, the half or game ends. A team timeout can avoid the runoff, but spending that timeout is itself a cost against the final drive. So the value of a challenge is not just P(reversal) times the swing in win probability from the corrected ruling; it must subtract the timeout's option value, the runoff risk, and the rhythm cost of a multi-minute stoppage for a quarterback operating a no-huddle tempo. The optimal policy is a threshold rule on the joint state: challenge only when the expected evidentiary clearance probability times the ruling's decision leverage exceeds the coupled resource cost. Late in a close game, the same spot error that is worth challenging at midfield in the second quarter can be worth accepting in the final two minutes, because the timeout capital is worth more than the half-yard. This is the precise sense in which the rulebook encodes a value-of-information problem with a shared budget constraint, and why naive 'always challenge when you think it is wrong' policies leak wins.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The challenge economy is scar tissue. The NFL ran a limited booth-only replay system from 1986 through 1991, reversing 376 of 2,967 reviews (p.43). On March 18, 1992, owners killed it: the vote was 17-11 in favor, short of the 21 required (chronology p.375), after six consecutive years of use. The scar was institutional - owners feared delay and the erosion of on-field authority. When replay returned on March 17, 1999, by a 28-3 vote (p.377), it came back as a coach-challenge system: paid, budgeted, and adversarial rather than free and centralized. In 2017 the league re-centralized rulings with officiating staff in New York (p.382). The hidden state in every modern challenge decision is that thirty-year oscillation between trust in officials and trust in video.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Three minds collide at the flag. The coach believes the spot is wrong and must simultaneously model the booth's evidence standard - his private certainty is not the booth's clear-and-obvious threshold, and confusing the two is the classic challenge leak. The defensive coordinator across the field models the coach's budget: with one challenge left and no successes, he expects hesitation on borderline plays and can tempo the next snap to exploit the doubt window before the flag. The quarterback's internal clock is the third mind: a long review stoppage cold-starts a rhythm offense, so the QB may privately prefer accepting a bad spot to buying a correction that kills his timing. The comfort call - hoard the timeout for the final drive - is rational for the clock but can be a trap when the spot error flips a fourth-down decision.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Physics and physiology veto the high-EV-looking challenge in specific states. With under ten seconds and no timeout, a failed challenge plus the 10-second runoff can end the half outright: the information purchase has negative expected value at any reversal probability, so the clock layer vetoes. Budget exhaustion vetoes next: no third challenge exists unless one of the first two succeeded, and a team out of timeouts pays 15 yards for even attempting. The physiological layer vetoes last: a rhythm quarterback's cold-start cost after a two-minute review can exceed the win-probability swing of a corrected half-yard spot, so the corrected ruling is not automatically the better outcome.

reasoning_traces.think: The overtime kernel on page 313 is a stopping rule with a path constraint, and its current form is the accumulated scar tissue of four rule eras. Read the terminal conditions carefully. In the 2025 alignment, both teams must possess or have the opportunity to possess, even if the first team scores a touchdown - but the first possession can still end the game if the defense scores a touchdown or the kicking team makes a safety on the receiving team's initial possession. After both opportunities, the next score by any method wins. In the regular season the whole process is capped at one 10-minute period, and a tie at the cap is a legal terminal state; in the postseason it runs in 15-minute periods until a winner, with the coin-toss loser gaining the kick/receive choice at the start of the third period if still tied. The definition of opportunity is narrow and kicking-play-specific: a kickoff is an opportunity for the receiving team; a legal kicking-team recovery counts as the opportunity consumed; a muffed punt or field goal beyond the line of scrimmage counts. A turnover on an ordinary scrimmage play does not, by itself, satisfy that definition. Now derive the policy consequences. Under the pre-2025 regular-season rule, a first-possession touchdown ended the game, so the receiving coach's opening drive carried terminal option value: a touchdown was not six points, it was the whole game. That inflated the value of aggressive fourth-down play and of big-play passing on the opening drive, and it made the coin toss enormously valuable. Under the 2025 kernel, the opening touchdown no longer terminates; the opponent answers. The opening drive's value reverts toward ordinary expected-points calculus plus the field-position externality of where the opponent will start. Fourth-down aggressiveness near midfield should be re-derived downward relative to the sudden-death era, while the kicking team's incentive to pin the opponent deep - because a safety on that initial possession still ends the game - rises. The coin toss value collapses toward the directional choice and the safety exception. The historical telemetry on page 312 shows why the rule kept changing: across all overtime games through 2024, 457 were won by field goal, 96 by touchdown pass, 57 by touchdown run, 21 by interception-return touchdown, and 29 ended tied. Field goals dominating the terminal-method distribution is exactly the fairness complaint that drove the 2010 postseason modification: a coin toss plus one long drive could decide a season without the opponent touching the ball. The 2025 alignment is the league paying down that fairness debt in the regular season too, at the cost of introducing the tie absorbing state more often, because ten minutes must now contain two possessions. For simulation, the kernel must be implemented as a hard terminal constraint with era tags: pooling pre-2025 regular-season overtime outcomes with post-2025 outcomes mixes two different stopping rules and will bias any estimated coin-toss or opening-drive effect.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The genealogy runs through four dated scars. December 28, 1958: Baltimore beat the Giants 23-17 in the first sudden-death overtime in an NFL Championship Game, Alan Ameche scoring after 8:15 of overtime (chronology p.368) - the broadcast-era legend that made sudden death sacred. 1974: one sudden-death period was added to preseason and regular-season games in a package explicitly adopted 'to add action and tempo' (p.371). March 23, 2010: owners amended postseason overtime to modified sudden death, guaranteeing a possession unless the receiving team scored a first-possession touchdown (p.380). 2022: postseason guaranteed both teams the ball even after a first-possession touchdown; 2025: the regular season aligned, with the 10-minute cap (p.313). Each rule is scar tissue over the previous rule's fairness failure.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The receiving coach now knows a touchdown will not end the game, so his opening-drive fourth-down calculus shifts: going for it on fourth-and-short near midfield is less attractive than in the sudden-death era, because the opponent gets the ball regardless and field position externalities dominate. The kicking coach knows the asymmetry that remains: a safety on the receiving team's initial possession still wins instantly, so deep pinning and coverage discipline carry terminal option value that ordinary expected-points models miss. The coin-toss winner's choice is now a belief about the opponent's opening-drive aggression and the wind, not about ending the game. Both coaches also model the clock: in the regular season, a long opening drive can consume the second team's guaranteed opportunity before it materializes, so tempo itself becomes a weapon against the guarantee.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The clock layer vetoes the fairness guarantee: ten minutes is a hard cap, and if the first possession runs long, the second team's opportunity can be truncated or never arrive - the guarantee is only as good as the remaining seconds. The fatigue layer vetoes postseason extrapolation: unbounded 15-minute periods degrade trench play and raise passing variance as duration grows (the longest postseason overtime ran 22:40, p.312), so regular-season-calibrated drive models misprice deep postseason overtime. The standings layer vetoes risk appetite: a tie is a legal terminal state worth half a win in the tiebreak mathematics (p.36 note), so a trailing coach's late-game aggression must be priced against the tie's standings value, not against a loss.

reasoning_traces.think: Two invariants in this book look like statistics but are actually constraint systems, and both fail in ways that matter for any engine that consumes them. The passer rating on page 314 is a bounded sensor. Its four components are each clipped to the interval from zero to 2.375, and the printed clamp notes make the saturation explicit: completion percentage above 77.5 earns no additional credit, touchdown percentage above 11.875 earns none, yards per attempt above 12.5 earns none, and any season without an interception already sits at the interception-component ceiling. The source even states its own exclusion clause: the system rates passers, not quarterbacks, and does not reflect leadership, play-calling, and other intangible factors. That is a printed admission that the observable is a projection of a higher-dimensional state, with the latent dimensions named. An engine that treats rating as a linear QB-quality feature commits two errors: it extrapolates through a region where the sensor's derivative is zero, and it imputes leadership from a statistic that provably does not contain it. The era problem compounds this: the fixed standard was calibrated on qualified passers since 1960 and adopted in 1973, but the 1978 rule package - defenders permitted contact with eligible receivers only once, head slap outlawed (chronology p.372) - structurally opened the passing game, so the same formula measures a different underlying distribution across eras. The tiebreak cascade on pages 36-37 fails differently. It is a non-Archimedean ordering: head-to-head results cannot be outweighed by any amount of point differential, because the criteria are consulted strictly in order and only until one separates the clubs. A team can outscore its opponents all season and still seed below a team it lost to twice. The subtler failure is implementation: the printed procedure is recursive, not a single lexicographic scan. When a club is eliminated, the remaining clubs restart at Step 1 of the applicable format - and the wild-card three-club case restarts at Step 2, not Step 1. A naive static argmax over the criteria vector will therefore mis-seed real tie configurations, because elimination order changes which criteria get applied to which subset. The terminal criterion is a coin toss, an irreducible random bit: deterministic ranking breaks down completely at step twelve, and the book's own chronology records a real instance, Carolina winning the 1995 draft coin toss with Jacksonville (p.376). The synthesis for the engine is a discipline of layers: use the rating only as a censored feature with era tags and separate latent channels for the named intangibles; implement seeding only through the recursive cascade with the random terminal node; and never let a scalar strength metric - Elo, point-differential models, weighted sums - veto either constraint, because both are higher-priority institutional invariants that sit above any statistical estimate in the decision hierarchy.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The rating's hidden state is its 1973 design intent: it replaced a method that ranked passers relative to their position in a total group, explicitly to remove inequities and allow cross-season comparison against a fixed standard built from qualified passers since 1960 (p.314). That fix froze the sensor while the game kept moving: the 1978 one-contact and head-slap reforms (p.372) and the 1994 two-point conversion and offensive package (p.376) changed the distribution the sensor measures. The tiebreak's hidden state is older: the league's first-ever first-place tie in 1932 forced an improvised extra game (p.365), and the cascade is the institutional memory of every since - a deterministic ordering built precisely because coin tosses and ad hoc extra games were judged unacceptable as routine arbiters.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The coach evaluates his quarterback on leadership and play-calling - the exact dimensions the rating's exclusion clause names - while the front office and the public argue from the rating, so the same player is two different objects in two different minds. The defensive coordinator exploits the formula's weighting: interceptions are the only negatively weighted component, and at 0.25 per percentage point they are weighted more heavily than touchdowns at 0.2, so pressure schemes that trade completions for interception risk attack the rating's weakest axis. The quarterback's internal clock pulls the other way: completion percentage rewards short, high-percentage throws, so a rating-optimal script can conflict with a win-optimal script that demands deep shots. The belief clash is structural, not interpersonal: each mind is optimizing a different projection of the same state.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The sensor layer vetoes extrapolation: above the 2.375 component caps the rating's derivative is zero, so any model that reads further improvement into a saturated component is fabricating signal; below one qualified attempt the formula is legal but meaningless, and the small-sample layer vetoes its use. The institutional layer vetoes the strength metric: head-to-head results sit above point differential in the cascade, so an engine's scalar strength estimate - however well calibrated - must never override the published seeding order. And the randomness layer vetoes determinism itself at step twelve: when the cascade reaches the coin toss, no amount of telemetry identifies the winner, and the honest engine output is a Bernoulli branch, not a point estimate.

universal_lens: The polymath audit lens this book trains is codified-procedure-as-invariant: decompose any competitive system into five layers - physical and geometric constraints, resource budgets (clock, timeouts, challenges, roster slots), evidence thresholds for state correction, terminal and stopping rules, and priority orderings for ties - then ask of any proposed advantage which layer it lives in and whether a higher-priority layer vetoes it. The NFL's rulebook is a century-long fossil record of exactly these layer conflicts, dated and voted on.
gsi_mapping: This book contains no biophysics, so the GSI transfer is explicitly structural, not sourced physiology: the clear-and-obvious reversal threshold is isomorphic to a specificity-weighted confirmatory diagnostic gate before intervention; the challenge-timeout budget maps to bounded clinical observation windows where monitoring consumes the same resource as treatment timing; the emergency third quarterback maps to reserve-capacity activation when primary pathways fail; both-possession overtime maps to crossover trial designs guaranteeing each arm exposure. Fluid and axonal-shear primitives must come from physiology sources, not this one.
gse_mapping: For the Coach-Mind simulator: implement the overtime stopping kernel and the recursive tiebreak cascade as hard constraints, the challenge economy as a value-of-information module with shared timeout capital, and the passer rating as a censored, era-tagged feature with separate latent channels for leadership and play-calling. Deception surfaces: model opponent challenge-budget exhaustion, third-quarterback cold starts, and opening-drive tempo attacks on the possession guarantee. DFS and portfolio tail risk: overtime variance, the tie absorbing state, and emergency-QB availability are roster-construction tail events. Internal artifacts only; no odds inputs; nothing published from this lane.
